newsitem.title: UK: Britain in new drive to ease mad cow export ban.
newsitem.headline: Britain in new drive to ease mad cow export ban.

text.p: Farm minister Jack Cunningham on Tuesday announced a new two-pronged effort to ease the European Union ban on Britain's beef exports and lighten the burden on its hard-pressed farmers.

London has been battling since March last year to persuade Brussels to allow its beef back into traditional markets around the world, but despite slaughtering thousands of animals at risk from "mad cow disease" has made no progress.
Last month EU veterinary scientists rejected a British proposal for a scheme allowing cattle from herds which never suffered from the fatal disease to be certified safe for export.
The scheme would initially have benefited Northern Irish herds because, unlike those in the rest of Britain, their movements have been tracked by computer records for the past eight years.

The EU vets said they were concerned about the government's ability to identify and trace all cattle at risk, but that if the proposals were amended to address five weaknesses which they identified, the scheme would prove acceptable.
Cunningham said in a parliamentary answer the proposal is now being revised to take account of the vets' criticisms.
"Eligibility for the scheme would be more restricted than originally proposed, but it would still be open in principle to producers in all parts of the United Kingdom," he said.

He said that in parallel the government was developing a new proposal for an export scheme based on the age of cattle, details of which would be announced after exploratory talks with the European Commission, the EU's executive arm.
Older cattle are at greater risk from the scheme since they are more likely to have eaten the contaminated feed which made it a big problem in Britain in the first place.
"We have put our ideas to the Commission about both schemes, and will press them with equal vigour," Cunningham said.
The EU slapped the ban on British exports after scientists found evidence that mad cow disease, bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), could be transmitted to humans as Creutzfeldt Jakob disease.
